This sight would have been unthinkable in 2016 when President Trump accused China of being a global pariah that was destroying America’s heartland. It also would have been unthinkable in 2020—that’s when Trump referred to the coronavirus as the “China Virus” and used a derogatory nickname for Covid-19 to blame Beijing for its spread.

   Not too far away on Wednesday evening, military officials were on their hands and knees smoothing and cleaning the airport red carpet before Xi walked across it. Making it just perfect.

   Why? Few know how to do domestic propaganda as well as the Chinese. 

   The images—of Chinese flags whipping in the wind, of Xi being toasted at a White House state dinner, or Chinese flags flying on the roof (!!) of the White House—will be played and replayed in Beijing for months and years (and decades?) to come. The Chinese Embassy in the U.S. tweeted up a storm Thursday, including many images of the national flag on display at the White House.

   To be sure, then-President Barack Obama hosted Xi to the White House twice, in 2015, and there were plenty of Chinese flags flying at 1600 Pennsylvania Ave. that day, too.

   Some Senate Republicans were livid at all the pomp this week, and this is truly a gamble for Trump.

   He similarly feted Russian President Vladimir Putin during a meeting in Anchorage last year. That event gave the Russians plenty of footage and images for domestic propaganda, but it didn’t lead to any changes in Russia’s war against Ukraine. Trump seems to be doubling down now, inviting Putin to the December G-20 summit in Florida.

   Will China be different? Could such flattery bring a modern China closer to the U.S. and pull it away from countries such as Russia and Iran? Or does it only embolden them more? Trump-Xi Summit Gives China Something Money Could Never Buy
 
Plus, the U.S. government paid for pro-Trump TV ad, and the White House restores access for reporters from CNN, MS NOW and Politico
 
 
EVAN VUCCI/REUTERS
 

Good morning. When I drove home Wednesday evening, traveling south down 14th Street N.W., people in light-blue hats exited buses and trucks carrying giant Chinese flags.

 

They had created a parade route of sorts for Chinese leader Xi Jinping on the streets of Washington. This sight would have been unthinkable in 2016 when President Trump accused China of being a global pariah that was destroying America’s heartland. It also would have been unthinkable in 2020—that’s when Trump referred to the coronavirus as the “China Virus” and used a derogatory nickname for Covid-19 to blame Beijing for its spread.

 

Not too far away on Wednesday evening, military officials were on their hands and knees smoothing and cleaning the airport red carpet before Xi walked across it. Making it just perfect.

 

Why? Few know how to do domestic propaganda as well as the Chinese. 

 

The images—of Chinese flags whipping in the wind, of Xi being toasted at a White House state dinner, or Chinese flags flying on the roof (!!) of the White House—will be played and replayed in Beijing for months and years (and decades?) to come. The Chinese Embassy in the U.S. tweeted up a storm Thursday, including many images of the national flag on display at the White House.

 

To be sure, then-President Barack Obama hosted Xi to the White House twice, in 2015, and there were plenty of Chinese flags flying at 1600 Pennsylvania Ave. that day, too.

 

Some Senate Republicans were livid at all the pomp this week, and this is truly a gamble for Trump.

 

He similarly feted Russian President Vladimir Putin during a meeting in Anchorage last year. That event gave the Russians plenty of footage and images for domestic propaganda, but it didn’t lead to any changes in Russia’s war against Ukraine. Trump seems to be doubling down now, inviting Putin to the December G-20 summit in Florida.

 

Will China be different? Could such flattery bring a modern China closer to the U.S. and pull it away from countries such as Russia and Iran? Or does it only embolden them more? Embolden them more to help Iran with satellite imagery? Embolden them more to help Iran evade sanctions? Embolden them more to resist Trump’s pressure on trade?

 

This is an edition of the Politics newsletter, bringing you an expert guide to what’s driving D.C. every day. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 
 
 

People and Policies I’m Watching

 

New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill: The Garden State’s governor is calling for the resignation of Lt. Gov. Dale Caldwell after an independent investigation found that Caldwell made a sexual comment to a staffer and tried to get a promotion for a romantic partner.

 

Trump’s Friday: This morning the president will have tea with Xi Jinping and his wife, Madame Peng Liyuan, then he will hold policy meetings this afternoon.

What I’m Following

 
 
BRENDAN SMIALOWSKI/AFP/GETTY IMAGES
 

The U.S. government paid for a pro-Trump TV ad. It opens with Trump saying, “Together we will defeat communism, Marxism in America once and for all.” The administration’s decision to fund an ad—it wouldn’t say how much it cost—that appears to include a voice clip from the Republican National Convention could violate federal law, ethics experts said.

 

Trump’s summit with Xi was heavy on ceremony and light on outcomes. Trump heralded the “tremendous strides” he and Xi had made, and Xi, through a translator, told Trump he was ready to work with him—and that two Chinese pandas would soon be sent to the Atlanta zoo. Meanwhile, the Trump administration has been quietly holding talks with China about its rapidly expanding nuclear arsenal.

 

The White House restored access Thursday morning to reporters from three outlets after a judge temporarily lifted Trump’s ban. U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, a Trump appointee, said administration officials had offered “little to back up their asserted national security interest” for instituting the ban. But then on Thursday night, MS NOW and CNN reported that some of their journalists were blocked from covering the guest arrivals portion of the state dinner honoring Xi.

 
 
 

What Else Is Happening

 

• A Big Tech industry group is urging the administration to withdraw its proposal to charge companies $103,265 for most new H-1B visa applications.

 

• Senate Republicans defeated a resolution to curb Trump’s ability to wage war against Iran, even as more GOP incumbents and candidates say they want the war to end soon.

 

• New York state sued Polymarket’s domestic arm, alleging that the bet-on-nearly-everything site was illegally running a gambling operation.

 

• A state judge ordered the Mamdani administration to produce any emails and text messages between top City Hall officials and an independent board that voted to freeze rents on New York City apartments.

• Texas Data Centers Face Investigation After Not Answering Water Questions (Dallas Morning News)

 
 
 

This Week in Washington History

 

In 1981, Sandra Day O’Connor was unanimously approved by the Senate as the first female Supreme Court justice. O’Connor retired in 2006 after nearly 25 years on the court, much of the time as its most powerful justice. She died in 2023 at the age of 93.
